The paper studies electromagnetic scattering from surfaces that are local perturbations of a fixed surface, consisting of finitely many 'bumps'.
Maxwell's equations are reduced to the form (Δ + k²)E = 0 with div E = 0 in R³\Ω, where k is the wave number.
The boundary condition is n×E|∂Ω = g, where n is the outward unit normal and g is a given tangential field in L²(∂Ω).
The Silver-Müller radiation condition is imposed at infinity to ensure uniqueness of the solution.
A Lipschitz domain is one where the boundary can be locally represented as the graph of a Lipschitz continuous function.
Non-tangential limits are used for all restrictions to the boundary, defined via the region Γ⁻(P) = {Y ∈ R³\Ω : |X-Y| < κ dist(Y,∂Ω)}.
The Maxwell Green matrix-valued function Γ⁰(X,Y) is a 3×3 matrix satisfying (ΔY + k²)Γ⁰(X,Y) = δX(Y)I₃.
The Maxwell Green function satisfies the symmetry property: Γ⁰(X₁,X₀) = [Γ⁰(X₀,X₁)]ᵗ.
The solution operator Q(f) is defined as Q(f)(X) = ∫∂Ω [∇Y Γ⁰(X,Y)]ᵗ f(Y) d∂(Y).
Q(f) automatically satisfies the Maxwell equations (Δ + k²)Q(f) = 0 and div Q(f) = 0 in R³\Ω.
The original surface ∂Ω₀ is partitioned into A (unperturbed portion) and B₀ (portion above which bumps are added).
The perturbed surface is ∂Ω = A ∪ B, where B represents the bumps and Ω₀ ⊆ Ω.
On the unperturbed portion A, the boundary behavior is: lim n(Z)×Q(f)(X) = f(Z).
On the perturbed portion B, the boundary behavior involves a jump condition with a -½ factor.
Proposition 4.2 establishes a key identity relating integrals over the entire boundary to integrals only over the bumps.
The main algorithm reduces the problem to solving a boundary integral equation only over the bumps B.
The algorithm requires knowledge of the Maxwell Green function for the original unperturbed surface Ω₀.
The approach is particularly useful when the underlying surfaces are slight perturbations of a fixed shape.
The paper builds on earlier work by the authors on similar algorithms for the scalar Helmholtz equation.
Working with vector-valued functions introduces new analytic and algebraic difficulties compared to scalar problems.
The boundary integral equation involves the operator n(Z)×[∇Y Γ⁰(Z,Y)]ᵗ acting on the unknown h.
The source term G(Z) in the boundary integral equation depends on both the boundary data g and the Green function.
The method is designed for implementation via boundary element methods in numerical applications.
The paper uses Green's formulas for vector fields to derive the main results.
The curl operator and its properties play a central role in the derivation of the algorithm.
